query: For W–Cu metal-matrix composites used in heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications, what single intervention could increase thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite, defines the application conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing an ultra‐thin nickel interphase layer at the tungsten–copper interfaces will reduce interfacial electron scattering, thereby increasing thermal conductivity while preserving mechanical durability and irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional W–Cu metal-matrix composite prepared without any interfacial modification, which typically exhibits relatively low thermal conductivity due to high electron scattering at the W/Cu boundaries.
generation.intervention: Deposit an ultra‐thin, uniform nickel layer (via chemical vapor deposition or another thin‐film technique) on the tungsten surfaces before copper is infiltrated or added during composite consolidation.
generation.conditions: The intervention is applicable under service conditions typical of heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications, namely elevated operating temperatures (e.g., 500–1000 °C) and exposure to irradiation environments that demand both high thermal transport and robust mechanical/structural integrity.
generation.structural_mediator: The nickel interphase serves as a chemically compatible binder at the W–Cu interfaces, promoting coherent bonding and reducing the mismatch in electron density and phonon spectra; this engineered interface minimizes electron scattering and interfacial thermal resistance while maintaining structural integrity under mechanical and irradiation stresses.
generation.mechanism: By introducing a nano-scale Ni layer, electron transmission across the interface is enhanced, leading to reduced interfacial thermal resistance and thus improved overall thermal conductivity. Simultaneously, nickel’s inherent mechanical strength and irradiation stability support durability, ensuring that the composite retains its mechanical performance and resistance to irradiation-induced microstructural damage.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified W–Cu composite, the Ni-coated composite will exhibit a measurable increase in thermal conductivity (with the magnitude to be determined by experiment, but expected to be a significant enhancement), while maintaining mechanical strength and irradiation resistance comparable to or better than the control.
generation.baseline: A conventional W–Cu composite without any interfacial modification, which suffers from higher electron scattering at the unmodified W/Cu interfaces and therefore lower thermal conductivity.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is limited to composites processed with a uniform, ultra-thin (<10 nm) Ni interphase layer and may not hold if the coating is too thick or discontinuous. The effects are predicted under high-temperature and irradiation conditions typical of fusion-reactor joints; different temperature ranges or irradiation regimes might alter performance.
generation.uncertainty: The exact degree of thermal conductivity improvement is uncertain until quantified; long-term stability of the Ni interphase under extended irradiation and cyclic thermal loading also requires further validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composite samples: one set with an ultra-thin Ni interphase layer deposited on tungsten surfaces before copper consolidation, and one set as an unmodified control. Subject both sets to cyclic thermal loading (in the 500–1000 °C range) and irradiation (simulating fusion-reactor conditions). Post-test, measure thermal conductivity, mechanical properties (e.g., tensile strength or bending tests), and microstructural integrity.
measurements: Thermal conductivity via laser flash analysis
Mechanical durability via standardized tensile/bending tests
Irradiation resistance and microstructural stability via transmission/scanning electron microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ni-coated composites fail to exhibit a statistically significant increase in thermal conductivity compared to the control, or if they show degraded mechanical strength or irradiation resistance, then the hypothesis is falsified.
